# Because of meditating on the Supreme, its powers are obscured; from that, indeed, come the soul's bondage and liberation. || 3.2.5 ||

|| 3.2.5 ||

It might be argued: the individual soul <term>jiva</term> is merely a part of the Supreme Self <term>para-atman</term>, like a spark from a fire. In that case, just as a fire and its sparks possess the same power of burning and illumination, the individual soul and the Lord <term>Ishvara</term> should both possess the powers of knowledge and sovereignty. Consequently, the soul would be capable of creating chariots and other objects in a dream through the mere power of its will <term>sankalpiki</term>. To this, we reply: while it is true that the individual soul and the Lord have a part-and-whole relationship, the fact that the soul possesses qualities contrary to those of the Lord is a matter of direct perception. Does the soul then lack the qualities of the Lord entirely? No, it is not that they are entirely absent; they exist, but are obscured by the obstruction of ignorance <term>avidya</term> and the like. This obscured power only manifests in a creature who, while meditating on the Supreme Lord and exerting the mind, has cleansed away the darkness—much like the power of vision, obscured by cataracts, is restored by the potency of medicine—and this happens only to those who have become perfected through the grace of the Lord, not to all creatures by nature. Why is this? Because from that, from the Lord as the cause, depend the bondage and liberation of this soul; bondage arises from the lack of knowledge of the Lord’s nature, and liberation arises from the knowledge of that nature. The scripture also says: "By knowing the Divine, all fetters fall away; with the fading of afflictions, birth and death cease. Through meditation on Him, in the third state at the dissolution of the body, one attains universal sovereignty and becomes fulfilled" <note>This refers to the Shvetashvatara Upanishad 1.11</note>, and so on.

# Or because of the connection to the body, that too. || 3.2.6 ||

|| 3.2.6 ||

Why then does the individual soul, while being a part of the Supreme Self, have its knowledge and sovereignty obscured? It is logical that knowledge and sovereignty should remain un-obscured, just as burning and illumination are in a spark of fire. We answer: this is true; however, that obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty occurs because of the connection to the body—the connection to the body, senses, mind, intellect, and the experience of objects. There is an analogy for this: just as the power of burning and illumination in a fire, though inherent, is obscured when it is contained within a piece of wood, or when it is covered by ashes, in the same way, the obscuration of the soul's knowledge and sovereignty arises from the connection to the limiting adjuncts <term>upadhi</term>—the body, name, and form—which are set up by ignorance, and from the confusion caused by distinguishing the soul from these. The word "or" <term>va</term> is used to ward off the doubt that the soul is distinct from the Lord. But, one might ask, could the soul be something other than the Lord, precisely because its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured; why posit a connection to the body? We reply: no, it is not reasonable for the soul to be other than the Lord. The scripture begins with "That Deity thought" <note>Referring to Chandogya Upanishad 6.3.2</note> and continues with "having entered by this individual soul as the self," referring to the soul with the word "Self" <term>atman</term>. Furthermore, it instructs the soul in its lordship, saying, "That is the Truth, that is the Self, That Thou Art, O Shvetaketu." Therefore, the soul is non-different from the Lord, and it is only because of the connection to the body that its knowledge and sovereignty are obscured. Consequently, the creation of chariots and such in a dream by the soul's will does not hold. If the creation of chariots in a dream were truly a matter of will, no one would ever experience an unpleasant dream, for no one wills an unpleasant thing. Regarding the argument that the scriptural mention of the waking state proves the reality of the dream state, such a comparison does not imply equal reality, as that would contradict the soul's nature as self-luminous, and the scripture itself shows the absence of actual chariots in a dream. Such a comparison is intended to show that the dream is like the waking state because it is caused by latent impressions <term>vasana</term> from the waking state. Therefore, it is established that the dream is mere illusion <term>maya-matram</term>.

# Its absence is in the channels, according to scripture, and in the Self. || 3.2.7 ||

The Section on Its Absence || 3.2.7 ||

The dream state has been examined; now the deep sleep state <term>sushupti</term> is being examined. There are these scriptural passages concerning deep sleep: in one place, it is heard, "When a person is thus asleep, fully integrated and serene, not knowing any dream, then he is asleep in the channels <term>nadi</term>." In another place, specifically mentioning the channels, it is heard, "Having glided through them, he rests in the pericardium <term>puritat</term>." Similarly, in another place, after mentioning the channels, it says, "He remains in them when he is asleep and does not see any dream, and then he becomes unified in the Vital Breath <term>prana</term> alone." Likewise, in another place, "He rests in that space which is within the heart." In another, "O Saumya, at that time he becomes united with the Being; he has attained his own Self." And also, "Embraced by the Prajna-Self, he knows nothing external or internal."

A doubt arises here: are these—the channels and the others—separate places of deep sleep independent of each other, or are they a single place of deep sleep, depending on one another? What is the conclusion? They are separate, because, since they have the same purpose, there is no interdependence between them.

<summary>Shankara explains that the soul's limited knowledge is an effect of its identification with the body, which obscures its inherent divine nature. He then transitions to the analysis of deep sleep, questioning whether various scriptural locations for this state—the channels, the heart, the pericardium, or the Supreme Being—are independent or unified.</summary>
